 Federal Film & TV Tax Credit Champ Steven Paul Tells AFM “We Have To Get This Accomplished Before The End Of The Year”

 L-R: Jon Voight, Steven Paul, Donald Trump and Scott Karol 
 Courtesy 
 In the wake of the blue wave hitting Congress , the drivers of the federal film and TV tax credit took the stage at the American Film Market on Tuesday to express their determination about getting the bill passed during the lame-duck session on Capitol Hill.
 Sitting on today’s panel were SP Media boss Steven Paul and SP Media COO Scott Karol , the special advisors to Donald Trump’s Hollywood ambassador Jon Voight ; as well as the MPA’s SVP of Federal Government Affairs, Josh Rogin.

 Rogin explained that the money the bill would yield runs out December 11; in order for the bill to push forward in Congress, it needs to attach itself to another bill, such as a tax extender.
 Watch on Deadline 
 “The biggest hurdle is finding something to attach it to,” Karol told us after the session. “It’s not going to be a stand-alone bill. It has to be part of something else. There are two options, the budget runs out on December 11, so there has to be sort of bill to fund the government. Query whether we can technically attach to that or not.”
 “The question is with the Democrats having the House and the Senate whether they will want to have a significant tax extender bill,” Karol told Deadline. 
 “We need to get this done while Donald Trump is in office,” Rogin emphasized. “He gives us the opportunity that we may not have at other times.”
 “We have to get this accomplished before the end of the year,” said Paul. “So, that we can start planning for 2027.”
 If the bill, which reportedly has 50 co-sponsors, is passed in December, it will take effect January 1.
 “If this doesn’t happen in December, then when will it take effect? Many films will be impacted,” said Karol. “At the end of the day, this is a jobs bill.”
 Rogin mentioned that the bill’s language could change: “We don’t want it to have a cap,” he said. He added that “Incoming speaker [Hakeem] Jefferies and majority leader [Chuck] Schumer support this, but we need them to make this a priority. It’s an opportunity that we can’t miss. We need them to put their back into it. It can’t just be a Republican ask, or a Democratic ask. A Democratic takeover isn’t bad for the prognosis of this bill.”
 Rogin pointed out that 39% of the U.S. film industry shoots stateside, down from 60% years ago.
 As previously reported, the proposed federal film and TV tax incentive starts at 20% for all labor spent on a film production. There are four 5% upticks, of which a production can only take advantage of two: a 5% uptick for a movie that qualifies as an independent production (meaning it’s not made by a publicly traded company), 5% for shooting 30% production days in a FEMA-declared disaster zone (which will help productions here in California areas impacted by fires) or rural zones; a 5% uptick for shooting in multiple jurisdictions; and a 5% credit if you’re a U.S. company bringing production back into the U.S. after previously shooting abroad.
 Note the proposed credit is on a production’s federal income tax. The federal incentive will set the floor upon which states can build their own programs.
 “It’s not a rebate” said Karol. “The producer who incurs the expense gets the deduction.”
 “You’re going to see a roar come into the industry like you’ve never seen before,” Paul said about once the tax credit is approved. “You’ll see investors, funds and banks come back to this industry, and I predict everyone will be want to be part of the entertainment business again.”
